findings.title: HTTP redirects to HTTPS
findings.description: Visitors who type or follow an http:// link should be sent to HTTPS immediately; otherwise traffic and cookies can be read or altered in transit.
findings.remediation: Add a site-wide permanent (301/308) redirect from http:// to https:// at the web server or CDN, then enable HSTS once every subdomain works over HTTPS.

findings.title: TLS certificate is valid and not close to expiry
findings.description: An invalid, mismatched or expired certificate triggers browser warnings and breaks API clients. Severity is high when verification fails or expiry is within 7 days, medium within 30 days.
findings.evidence: Plain-HTTP target on a non-default port; TLS not applicable.
findings.remediation: Renew or reissue the certificate, make sure it covers the exact hostname, and automate renewal (for example ACME/Let's Encrypt with monitoring on expiry).

findings.title: HSTS is enabled with a long max-age
findings.description: Strict-Transport-Security tells browsers to use HTTPS only, which defeats downgrade and cookie-stripping attacks. A max-age under 180 days is considered too short to be effective.
findings.evidence: Homepage is not served over HTTPS; HSTS is ignored on HTTP.
findings.remediation: Send 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains' on HTTPS responses. Start with a short max-age while testing, then raise it.

findings.title: Content-Security-Policy is set and not trivially bypassable
findings.description: CSP limits where scripts and other resources may load from, which is the main browser-side mitigation for cross-site scripting. Policies that allow 'unsafe-inline', 'unsafe-eval' or wildcards for scripts give little protection.
findings.remediation: Start with 'Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only', collect violations, then enforce a policy such as "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'self'".

findings.title: Clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors)
findings.description: Without framing protection another site can embed this one in an invisible frame and trick users into clicking.
findings.remediation: Send "Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'" (preferred) and/or 'X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN' for older browsers.

findings.title: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
findings.description: Stops browsers from guessing content types, which can turn uploads into scripts.
findings.remediation: Send 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' on all responses.

findings.title: Referrer-Policy limits URL leakage
findings.description: The Referer header can leak full URLs (including tokens in query strings) to third parties. A restrictive policy keeps that data on your own origin.
findings.remediation: Send 'Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin' (or stricter).

findings.title: Permissions-Policy is set
findings.description: Permissions-Policy disables browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation...) the site does not need, limiting the impact of injected or third-party content.
findings.remediation: Send e.g. 'Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()'.

findings.title: Cross-origin isolation headers (COOP/CORP/COEP)
findings.description: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy isolate the page from other origins. They are defence in depth and not required for every site, so this is informational.
findings.remediation: Consider 'Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin' and 'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site' if the site does not rely on cross-origin popups or embeds.

findings.title: Server header does not disclose a version
findings.description: Version banners make it trivial to look up known vulnerabilities for the exact software in use.
findings.remediation: Hide versions: 'server_tokens off;' (nginx), 'ServerTokens Prod' and 'ServerSignature Off' (Apache), or strip the header at the CDN/proxy.

findings.title: No framework banner headers (X-Powered-By and friends)
findings.description: Headers such as X-Powered-By, X-AspNet-Version and X-Generator advertise the technology stack and often its version.
findings.remediation: Remove the headers: 'expose_php = Off' for PHP, 'header_remove("X-Powered-By")', or 'proxy_hide_header X-Powered-By;' in nginx.

findings.title: Cookies have the Secure flag
findings.description: Cookies without Secure may be sent over plain HTTP, where they can be read or replaced by anyone on the network path. Session-like cookie names raise the severity.
findings.evidence: Homepage is served over HTTP, where Secure cannot take effect.
findings.remediation: Set the Secure attribute on every cookie (framework session settings usually expose it).

findings.title: Cookies have the HttpOnly flag
findings.description: HttpOnly hides a cookie from JavaScript, so an XSS bug cannot steal it. Session-like cookie names raise the severity.
findings.remediation: Set HttpOnly on session and authentication cookies.

findings.title: Cookies declare SameSite
findings.description: SameSite=Lax or Strict stops browsers attaching the cookie to cross-site requests, reducing cross-site request forgery. SameSite=None requires Secure.
findings.evidence: Cookies without a safe SameSite: session_hint
findings.remediation: Set 'SameSite=Lax' (or 'Strict' where possible) on cookies.

findings.title: No exposed .git directory
findings.description: A web-accessible .git directory lets anyone download the repository, including history, configuration and sometimes credentials.
findings.remediation: Deploy build artefacts, not working copies. Block dot-directories at the web server ('location ~ /\. { deny all; }'), and rotate any secret that was ever committed.

findings.title: No exposed .env file
findings.description: Environment files commonly hold database passwords, API keys and app secrets.
findings.remediation: Move the file outside the web root or deny access to it, then rotate every secret it contained: assume it was read.

findings.title: No backup or archive files in the web root
findings.description: Database dumps, archives and *.bak copies of configuration files are downloadable by anyone who guesses the name, and often contain credentials or full site content.
findings.remediation: Delete the files, store backups outside the web root, and add a deploy-time check that fails if archives or *.bak/*.old/*~ files appear in the published directory.

findings.title: Directory listing is disabled
findings.description: Directory indexes reveal file names (backups, exports, uploads) that should not be discoverable.
findings.remediation: Disable auto-indexing ('autoindex off;' in nginx, 'Options -Indexes' in Apache).

findings.title: No diagnostic or admin-tool leftovers (phpinfo, server-status, Adminer)
findings.description: phpinfo() pages, Apache server-status and database admin tools expose configuration details and attack surface to the whole internet.
findings.remediation: Remove the files, or restrict them by IP/VPN and authentication. Never leave diagnostics on production.

findings.title: WordPress version is not disclosed
findings.description: The <meta name='generator'> tag advertises the exact WordPress version, which makes targeted attacks against outdated installs easier.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Remove the generator tag (remove_action('wp_head', 'wp_generator')) and, more importantly, keep core updated so the version does not matter.

findings.title: xmlrpc.php is not reachable
findings.description: xmlrpc.php enables password guessing at scale (system.multicall) and pingback abuse. Most sites do not need it. Only a GET is sent; the endpoint's standard 'POST only' answer is enough to prove it is live.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Block /xmlrpc.php at the web server or with a hardening plugin, unless a specific integration (such as the mobile app or Jetpack) requires it.

findings.title: REST API does not list users publicly
findings.description: /wp-json/wp/v2/users (or /?rest_route=/wp/v2/users) returns user slugs (often the login name) to anonymous visitors, giving attackers half of every credential pair.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Restrict the users endpoint to authenticated requests (a small mu-plugin using the rest_endpoints filter, or your security plugin) and make sure login names differ from public author slugs.

findings.title: ?author=N does not reveal usernames
findings.description: Requesting /?author=1 redirects to /author/<login>/ on default installs, revealing the username of the first account.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Redirect or 404 ?author= queries for anonymous visitors, or set a different user_nicename so the slug is not the login.

findings.title: readme.html / license.txt are not exposed
findings.description: readme.html shows the installed version and confirms the platform.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Delete readme.html and license.txt (WordPress restores them on updates, so block them at the server instead).

findings.title: wp-content/debug.log is not exposed
findings.description: With WP_DEBUG_LOG enabled, PHP errors (paths, queries, sometimes personal data) are written to a file that is publicly downloadable by default.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Delete the file, set WP_DEBUG_LOG to a path outside the web root (or disable it), and deny access to *.log files.

findings.title: wp-login.php is reachable from the internet
findings.description: The login page is expected on most sites, but it is the main target of password guessing. This is a note, not a vulnerability.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Add rate limiting or a WAF rule, enforce strong passwords and two-factor authentication, and consider restricting /wp-admin by IP or VPN for editors.

findings.title: Plugin and theme names are not enumerable from page source
findings.description: Asset URLs reveal which plugins and themes are installed. This is detection only: SiteCheckup does not look versions up in vulnerability databases. Exposed versions raise the severity to low.
findings.evidence: WordPress was not detected on the homepage.
findings.remediation: Keep every plugin and theme updated and remove unused ones. Hiding names is not a substitute for patching.

findings.title: robots.txt is present
findings.description: robots.txt tells well-behaved crawlers what to skip and where the sitemap is. It is not an access control: never list secret paths in it.
findings.remediation: Publish /robots.txt with a Sitemap: line and sensible Disallow rules.

findings.title: security.txt is published
findings.description: RFC 9116 security.txt gives researchers a clear, private channel to report problems.
findings.evidence: No security.txt with a Contact field found.
findings.remediation: Publish /.well-known/security.txt with Contact: and Expires: fields.

findings.title: No mixed content on the homepage
findings.description: Scripts, frames and stylesheets loaded over http:// from an HTTPS page can be tampered with (medium); images and media are lower risk (low).
findings.evidence: Homepage is not served over HTTPS.
findings.remediation: Change the references to https:// (or protocol-relative paths), fix hard-coded URLs left over from migrations in the database/templates, and add 'upgrade-insecure-requests' to the CSP as a safety net.

findings.title: Homepage has sensible cache headers
findings.description: Responses without any caching headers are re-downloaded every time; responses that set cookies but are marked public can be cached by shared proxies and leak between users.
findings.evidence: Response sets cookies but is publicly cacheable: public, max-age=300
findings.remediation: Send an explicit Cache-Control: 'public, max-age=...' for static pages, 'private, no-store' for anything personalised or that sets session cookies.
